analysis.one_liner: Forces federal storage of nuclear plant waste in Nevada by 1999 while limiting lawsuits and environmental review.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed it 63–37 on July 31, 1996, but the House never voted on it, and it died when that Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill ordered the Energy Department to start taking radioactive spent fuel from the nation's nuclear power plants by November 1999, storing it at an interim site next to the proposed Yucca Mountain repository in Nevada. It set a hard federal deadline, cut off the government's liability for missing deadlines, released utilities from further payment obligations for older fuel, and sharply limited court challenges and environmental review. It preempts state and local law and routes all lawsuits to federal appeals courts, which could not halt construction of the facility.
analysis.who_benefits: Operators of the nation's civilian nuclear power reactors. They had contracted in the 1980s for the federal government to take their spent fuel, and were storing it on-site and suing the Energy Department over missed deadlines. The bill set a firm 1999 acceptance date, shielded the government from liability for missing deadlines, and let utilities that paid a one-time fee walk away from all future storage and disposal obligations [S2][S4]. It also directed the Energy Department to use private contractors to the maximum extent possible [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Energy Department to begin storing utilities' spent nuclear fuel at an interim facility in Nevada no later than November 30, 1999, removing waste that utilities were keeping at their own plants [S2].

Shields the United States from any financial liability if the Energy Department misses acceptance or emplacement deadlines, settling the utilities' delay disputes on terms favorable to the federal side of the bargain while still forcing a pickup date [S2].
Provides that a one-time fee for fuel used before 1983 relieves the payer of any further financial obligation for long-term storage or permanent disposal [S2].
Directs the Energy Department to use private-sector management and contracting to the maximum extent possible in running the waste program [S2].

Narrows the licensing standards: the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's public-protection finding is based on a single overall performance standard, and the environmental review may not consider the need for the facility, alternative sites, or alternative designs [S3][S4].

analysis.who_pays: Nevada residents, who would host a high-level waste storage facility at the Nevada Test Site before a permanent repository is proven, and communities along the rail and highway routes in many states that the waste would travel. The bill preempts state and local law and channels all legal challenges to federal appeals courts, leaving affected states and tribes with little recourse. Ratepayers continue paying the nuclear waste fee through their electric bills.
analysis.who_pays_short: Nevadans and communities along waste routes

drawbacks.text: Thousands of shipments of spent nuclear fuel and high-level waste would move by rail and truck from plants across the country to Nevada starting in 1999, before any permanent repository is demonstrated to work [S2][S3].

The bill preempts state and local law, gives federal appeals courts original and exclusive jurisdiction over all cases, and bars any court from stopping construction or operation of the interim storage facility before licensing review concludes [S2][S4].

It limits environmental review: no environmental impact statement before key siting and design decisions, and the final statement may not consider the need for the facility, alternatives to it, or alternative sites [S4].
The government is ordered to accept waste on a fixed schedule while being shielded from liability for failing to meet that schedule, an asymmetry an honest supporter would have to acknowledge [S2].

It locks in a single site: site work on any second repository is prohibited unless Congress specifically authorizes and funds it, committing the country to one location in Nevada before its viability is established [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The problem the bill addressed was real: nuclear plants were storing spent fuel on-site, and the Energy Department had missed its contractual promise to take it. But the bill solved that on the industry's terms — a firm pickup deadline and release from further fees for utilities, paid for by Nevada and transport-route communities through a facility sited before a permanent repository is proven, with environmental review narrowed, state law preempted, and courts barred from halting the project. A more balanced approach would have tied interim storage to a proven disposal path and preserved ordinary legal and environmental checks.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it 63–37 on July 31, 1996, but the bill sat at the House desk for two months, was referred to three committees in October, and died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997 without a House vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Larry Craig introduced the bill on July 9, 1996, with 13 cosponsors (12 Republicans and 1 Democrat) [S1][S5].
On July 16, the Senate invoked cloture on the motion to proceed 65–34 (Republicans 50–2, Democrats 15–32), and the motion to proceed was then withdrawn as the measure was laid before the Senate [S7].
On July 31, 1996, the Senate passed the bill with amendments 63–37 (Republicans 50–3, Democrats 13–34) [S8].

The House received the bill on August 1, 1996, and held it at the desk; on October 4 it was referred to the Commerce, Resources, and Transportation and Infrastructure Committees, and on November 1 to the Energy and Power Subcommittee. No House vote ever occurred, and the Congress ended January 3, 1997 [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nevadans and communities along potential waste transport routes are better off because the bill never became law. Nuclear plant operators gained nothing from the outcome and continued storing spent fuel on-site while the Energy Department's disposal program remained stalled.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nevadans and communities along waste routes

sides.party_line_note: Nearly all Republicans backed the bill (50–3 on final passage, 50–2 on cloture) while most Democrats opposed it (13–34 on final passage, 15–32 on cloture), with roughly a quarter of Senate Democrats crossing over.

industries.note: The bill required the federal government to take their spent fuel by November 1999 and released pre-1983 fuel owners from all further disposal obligations. The cost of the waste program's siting, transportation risks, and preempted state oversight fell on Nevada and communities along shipping routes [S2].

industries.industry: Nuclear waste transport and storage contractors
industries.note: The bill directed the Energy Department to use private-sector participation to the maximum extent possible and to procure U.S.-made transport systems, creating federal contracts for storage, handling, and shipment of high-level waste [S2].

industries.industry: State and local governments along transport routes
industries.note: The bill preempted state and local law in favor of the federal act and channeled all litigation to federal appeals courts, stripping states and tribes along shipping routes of ordinary legal recourse, though it offered training funds and public education programs in return [S2][S4].
